newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak parliament halts bank selloffs until 2003.
newsitem.headline: Slovak parliament halts bank selloffs until 2003.

text.p: The Slovak parliament on Thursday approved a measure effectively halting bank privatisation until the end of the year 2003 at the earliest.
The law was passed by 75 votes in favour, 64 against and three abstentions of the 143 deputies present. One deputy did not vote.
"The law bars privatisation of shares owned by the state or the National Property Fund (the state privatisation agency)," the law says.

Through the NPF, the state controls 91.3 percent of the largest savings bank Slovenska Sporitelna, 50.5 percent in the major insurance company Slovenska Poistovna, some 35 percent in bank IRB and about 17 percent in the largest commercial bank VUB.
The Czech National Property Fund also holds about 33 percent in VUB.
"We are not against bank privatisation, but the banks have to be first restructured under state supervison," said Brigita Schmoegnerova of the opposition Party of the Democratic Left (SDL).
Schmoegnerova said it would be necessary to work out a new banking law prior to the bank sell-off after the year 2003.

Last June, bank privatisation was at the heart of a crisis within Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's ruling coalition consisting of his Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), the ultra-right Slovak National Party and the ultra-left Workers' Party (ZRS) which was against the selloff.
The rift was eventually settled and parliament then approved a measure postponing the bank privatisation until March 31, 1996.
Political and economic analysts say the current row over banking privatisation inside the coalition may indicate another serious crisis between the coalition parties.
All 12 deputies of ZRS today joined the parliamentary opposition, which drafted the legislation, and voted for postponement of the bank selloff.
The government has said it was necessary to privatise the banks as soon as possible to fulfil conditions for membership into international economic organisations, such as the OECD.
The OECD, however, last year warned Slovakia against too quick a bank selloff, saying the restructuring of state- controlled financial institutions was more crucial.
